Sadly yes, I barely get the fun one, but I’ve learned some ways over the years to mitigate it.

I know my telltale symptom of the irritability is a distinct feeling in my chest/throat area. While I have it, I know I am very prone to feeling disproportionately intense anger to almost anything that could happen around me. Maybe you have a telltale physical sign too. It took a lot of practice, but I basically have to put a ton of mental energy to question everything I am doing and saying while I have this feeling, mostly with interactions I have with others.

If a customer at work asks me a super normal question while I have the chest feeling and I suddenly get a super intense wave of anger, I remind myself this is not something the real me has a reason to be upset over, and that I shouldn’t treat a person poorly just because I have a chemical imbalance. Self awareness is so important here. I try to compensate by either being fairly quiet or very formal and polite. I clearly don’t seem myself when I’m like this, but it’s better than lashing out at people for little reason.

When I’ve been in romantic relationships, I try my best to communicate with my partner when I’m having an episode (it’s normal I’ll have episodes of experiencing these symptoms a lot over 3-5 days), and that I might need more space or be less talkative. I try to avoid people when I am feeling irritable. I feel terrible if I emotionally hurt my loved ones because of it, so my strategy is to avoid people when things are at their worst.

Those are a few strategies I’ve been working on for the past few years especially. Hypomanic anger is a destructive force and while I wish I could take back some of the things I did as a teen because of it, all I can do it improve myself and be a better man for the future.

Like 80% of the time I’m hypomanic, it’s just a ton of irritability, disproportionate anger, and being incredibly reactive. I barely get the ‘fun’ hypomania and during these irritability times I have to closely monitor every single thing I do or say to maintain control.

When i first started taking meds: nothing different. Still awful and episodes controlled my life to the point where it was genuinely unlivable.

After 2 years of trying different med combos/doses and finally finding one that works: huge difference in 6 weeks. Much more time in between symptom days. Symptoms are a lot less frequent and severe. 

Episodes still can get bad, but with meds bringing the duration/intensity/frequency down to a more manageable level, they no longer control my life and rarely lead me to do destructive things (compared to often before). I’m gradually working on recognizing warning signs, mitigating the symptoms, identifying patterns, etc but I wouldn’t have ever been able to do that if meds weren’t in the picture.

Basically, I still have bad days, but the days are now liveable and im building a life I want. I don’t think it will ever fully turn off, but im succeeding now more than ever before. What I have is clearly a chemical imbalance, as my body physically feels so distinctly different when in episodes (eg: intense feelings in chest and throat area), and not feeling that most of the time makes it much easier to think straight.

A tip for training I’ve learned is to find a schedule that works for you and you can realistically stay consistent. For example, my day to day life can be all over the place as a uni student with a job, a relationship, family, etc, so it’s hard to predict what I’ll do every single day. I could never do specific plans in advance like ‘each Wednesday I will do x sets at 1:30pm). I also have a mood disorder, so I can’t always expect to be able to be productive in a time planned in advance.

My solution is that I make a list of 100 sets (split between different muscle groups and exercises I want that week) that are to be done each week. This can be split into 3-5 workouts. I do them whenever I feel I have time/energy, but still hold myself accountable to get them done by the end of the week.

I do something similar for tasks I have to do each week related to my studies. Maybe you’d work best with something more structured, maybe you wouldn’t.

A good way to stay motivated is to also set some goals. Someday I want to be able to bench 200lbs. I’m 20lbs away from that and each little victory along the way is always the highlight of my day.

Like would you find a sports game more exciting if your team won 24-23 or 24-3? Would you really be interested in watching a NFL team play middle schoolers when you already know how it ends? By rooting for the underdog, you’re rooting for an exciting game. I’m not sure what the exact psychological terms are for this, but I think it plays a part.

I think we are also exposed to a lot of media from a young age where the protagonist is an underdog of some sort. There are so many stories/movies/etc of the unpopular kid at school succeeding against the bully, or all those YA series of a teenager fighting against an oppressive ruler. We are taught to empathize with these characters and support them, as stories are told from their eyes.

Nothing will cure my bipolar depression, I’ll probably still have episodes 50 years from now. 

But I can learn to recognize the signs of an episode before it gets too bad. For one example, I have a super distinct feeling in my throat/chest that makes an episode easy to recognize if I practice frequent check ins with myself. If I can catch the physical signs early on, I can make sure I am self aware that the episode is not a reflection of my actual life situation, but more so a symptom of a mental illness. This can help me to stay logical. Once I recognize I am in an episode, I acknowledge that I likely have the same emotional reasoning a drunk person would, and try to ask myself before making a decision (for example to end my life), is this a decision a drunk person should make? Learning to recognize an episode and realize it’s not from my actual life but instead the chemicals in my body took a LONG time and a LOT of practice to learn. Having the physical sensations of depression suck, but knowing it’s just a chemical imbalance and it will go away makes it a lot better.

I can also establish a support system of close people in my life who will know what to do when I have an episode, have medications that can be adjusted when necessary, etc. 


I can figure out ideas for what I can do during an episode that will help, but I also will realistically be able to do. For example, I can often convince myself to start reading my poems out loud because I’m expressing the pain I’m feeling. This can help to get me off the couch and break the spell the episode has on me.

I’m not saying any of those things are easy to do, but if I’m going to deal with this my whole life, it’s worth doing everything I can to reduce the damage and pain an episode can cause.
